quoted_clause: cap T, cache prefixes, or quantize KV (FP8), as these levers can repeatedly beat adding hosts on price — each relaxes the KV-capacity ceiling without commissioning new hardware
observed: The sentence says prefix caching relaxes the KV-capacity ceiling, but earlier text says prefix caching does not reduce the request's own KV-resident context.
evidence: §6 states: 'prefix caching reduces recomputation and shares prefix KV but does not by itself reduce the request's own KV-resident context.' Prefix caching can reduce aggregate shared-prefix KV and recomputation, but not per-request KV residency.
root_cause: Overgeneralizing three different levers into one claim.
correction: Distinguish: cap T/compaction/quantization reduce per-request KV; prefix caching can reduce aggregate recomputation and shared-prefix KV but not the request's own KV-resident context.
acceptance_test: The sentence no longer says prefix caching relaxes the per-request KV ceiling; it states the aggregate/shared-prefix qualification.

quoted_clause: The event-level ledger below derives `task_input`, `task_output`, peak residency, and billed tokens for the T = 3 trace under a stated cache policy.
observed: The ledger table has no billed-token column and no stated cache policy; billed tokens are only discussed later as provider-dependent.
evidence: The table columns are Call, Input before call, New model output, Tool output, Post-call retained context. No billed column or cache-rate assumption appears.
root_cause: Ledger introduction promises a quantity the ledger does not derive.
correction: Remove 'billed tokens' from the sentence or add a billed-token column with an explicit cache/billing assumption.
acceptance_test: The ledger introduction matches the table columns and any stated cache policy.

quoted_clause: the execution-trace totals for the same T are 19,265 / 30,195 / 41,990
observed: These are task_input totals, not total execution-trace tokens; total tokens would include output 365 / 430 / 495.
evidence: §4 ledger gives task_input = 19,265 / 30,195 / 41,990 and task_output = 365 / 430 / 495 for T=1/2/3. The footnote calls the input-only values 'execution-trace totals'.
root_cause: Labeling input-only totals as total execution-trace totals.
correction: Call them 'task_input totals' or include the output totals.
acceptance_test: The footnote label matches the values; if it says 'totals', the values include output.

quoted_clause: input tokens/call × $/in token + output tokens/call × $/out token + cached tokens/call × $/cached token
observed: The cost equation adds cached tokens as a separate term alongside input tokens without defining whether input tokens/call excludes cached tokens.
evidence: Cached tokens are normally a subset of input tokens. If input tokens/call includes cached tokens, adding cached tokens/call × $/cached token double-counts them unless $/cached token is a differential price and input tokens/call is uncached-only.
root_cause: Undefined token categories in the cost equation.
correction: Define input tokens/call as uncached input and add cached tokens/call separately, or use a single input term with the appropriate blended cache price.
acceptance_test: The equation's token categories are mutually exclusive and sum to billed input tokens; a worked substitution shows no double-counting.

observed: The arrow-and-value fragment '→ 22 hosts.' is duplicated immediately after itself, producing '→ 22 hosts.→ 22 hosts.'
evidence: Literal duplication in the source text; the second occurrence adds no information and reads as a copy/paste artifact.
root_cause: Editing residue from a prior revision where the sentence was reflowed.
correction: Delete the second '→ **22 hosts**.' so the sentence ends once: '... ≈ 21.3 → **22 hosts**.'
acceptance_test: Grep for '22 hosts.→ 22 hosts' returns zero hits; the ρ-derate sentence ends with a single '22 hosts'.

observed: The derived low-end rate (~9 Gb/s at 120 s) falls below the stated path minimum of ~10 Gb/s. The 120 s load time implies a rate outside the quoted path range.
evidence: 140 GB / 120 s = 1.167 GB/s = 9.33 Gb/s < 10 Gb/s. The 30 s end (37 Gb/s) is inside the range; the 120 s end is not.
root_cause: The load-time range and the path-rate range were chosen independently and are not mutually consistent at the slow end.
correction: Either widen the path range to '~9–40 Gb/s' or tighten the load-time range to '30–110 s' (140/110 = 1.27 GB/s = 10.2 Gb/s). State that the achieved rate is ~90% of the path rate to make the relationship explicit.
acceptance_test: The derived Gb/s range is a subset of the stated path range, or the text explicitly notes the ~90% efficiency gap.

quoted_clause: the larger requirement wins — 21 hosts under case (i), 22 under case (ii); with the standalone ρ = 0.95 derate applied to the prefill screen ... case (ii) rises to ⌈21.81 / 0.95⌉ = 23 hosts
observed: The summary enumerates case (i) and case (ii) but omits case (iii), even though case (iii) was computed two paragraphs earlier (21 hosts prefill screen, max with 21 KV screen = 21).
evidence: Case (iii) prefill screen = ⌈20.21⌉ = 21; KV screen = 21; max = 21. The summary's '21 under case (i), 22 under case (ii)' is incomplete without noting case (iii) also yields 21.
root_cause: The summary was written for the two cases that produce distinct maxima and did not reconcile with the three-case enumeration above.
correction: Add case (iii) explicitly: '21 hosts under case (i), 21 under case (iii), 22 under case (ii)'. Or state that case (iii) coincides with case (i) at 21.
acceptance_test: All three FLOP-counting cases appear in the max-over-screens summary, or the text explicitly says case (iii) coincides with case (i).

quoted_clause: the same demand ÷ ceiling in PFLOP/s: 2 × 1.5099 ÷ 2.7692, with 2.7692 PFLOP/s the Chapter 8 35%-MFU host peak
observed: The notation '2 × 1.5099' is cryptic: 1.5099 is the case-(ii) prefill demand per FLOP-per-token-per-parameter (1.288 × 1.1723), and the leading '2' is the FLOPs-per-token-per-parameter factor. A reader cannot recover this from the sentence alone.
root_cause: The intermediate quantity 1.5099 is introduced without its units or derivation, and the '2 ×' factor is not labeled.
correction: Expand to: 'the same demand ÷ ceiling in PFLOP/s: (2 FLOP/token/param × 1.288 PFLOP/s × 1.1723) ÷ 2.7692 PFLOP/s = 3.0198 ÷ 2.7692 ≈ 109%'. Or drop the parenthetical and rely on the token-rate ratio already given.
acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce 3.0198 PFLOP/s from the printed expression without consulting Chapter 8.

page_hint: Ch 20 §2 and §3, '1.08 s prefill' vs '19,780 tokens/s ceiling'
quoted_clause: a ~8.6 s service time per request (1.08 s prefill + ~7.5 s decode)
observed: The text presents 1.08 s as the per-request prefill time, but at 2.0 req/s this implies 2.16 request-seconds of prefill per second (>100% of a serial prefill engine). The reconciliation — that prefill is batched with batch size ≈2.16 — is never stated. Separately, 1.08 s for 9,200 tokens is 8,519 tokens/s, i.e. 43% of the 19,780 tokens/s ceiling, which is consistent with batching but not explained.
evidence: 2.0 req/s × 1.08 s = 2.16 concurrent prefill requests; 9,200/1.08 = 8,519 tokens/s per request; 18,400/19,780 = 93% aggregate. The numbers close only if prefill is batched.
root_cause: The service-time decomposition is presented as if prefill were serial, while the throughput arithmetic silently assumes batched prefill.
correction: Add one sentence in §3: 'The 1.08 s prefill is the batched prefill latency at the steady-state batch size (~2.16 requests); a single-request prefill at the 19,780 tokens/s ceiling would take ~0.47 s, and the gap is the achieved-MFU shortfall.'
acceptance_test: The text explicitly reconciles the per-request prefill latency with the aggregate prefill ceiling, or the 1.08 s figure is relabeled as batched.

quoted_clause: Dividing the total by the ~9,500 tokens/request gives ~3.7 requests/s
observed: The text uses '~3.7 requests/s' here and '3.684' in the next paragraph ('⌈40 / 3.684⌉ = 11 hosts'). Both are correct (3.684 ≈ 3.7), but the precision switch without a note is a minor inconsistency.
root_cause: Two different roundings of the same quotient appear in adjacent paragraphs.
correction: Use '3.684' consistently, or write '~3.7 (3.684 unrounded)' at first use and reuse 3.684 thereafter.
acceptance_test: The same quotient is printed with one precision throughout §3.

page_hint: Ch 21 §3, 'Cost of a bad ungated release'
observed: The printed dollar results are correct for requests × ($/1K) / 1000, but the displayed formula divides by 1,000 twice. As written, the formula yields about $5.39 and $3.03, not $5,394 and $3,032.
root_cause: Double division by 1,000 in the displayed cost formula.
correction: Write 216,000/1,000 × $24.97 ≈ $5,394, or 216,000 × $24.97/1K without the extra ÷1,000. Apply the same fix to the $14.038/1K line.
acceptance_test: Recompute both lines from the displayed formula; the result must equal the printed dollar amount and carry dollar units.

quoted_clause: No fire drill, no user-visible regression, no manual heroics — the factory made the wrong vendor claim cost nothing to the business
observed: The same mini-case reports 12 legal-subset failures among 3,600 canary requests. If the 5% canary is production traffic, those 12 are user-visible failures; the claim of zero user-visible regression and zero business cost contradicts the reported canary outcome.
evidence: Canary served 3,600 requests; 12 legal-subset failures; legal subset ≈360 requests. A canary serving real traffic cannot have both 12 failures and no user-visible regression.
root_cause: Conflates 'contained blast radius' with 'zero impact'.
correction: Say the regression was contained to the canary (12 users affected) and production-wide impact was avoided; or explicitly define the canary as shadow/internal traffic if zero user impact is intended.
acceptance_test: The mini-case either reports the 12 canary failures as user-visible but contained, or explicitly states the canary was shadow traffic; it does not claim zero user-visible impact while reporting failures.

page_hint: Ch 22 §3, 'The loop on a second workload'
quoted_clause: KV footprint per request is 2.62 MB × 400 ≈ 1.05 GB rather than ~24.1 GB
observed: For the stated 400-input/900-output workload, the KV cache at end of turn is 2.62 MB × (400+900) ≈ 3.41 GB, not 1.05 GB. The canonical table uses 9.5K max for 9.2K input + 300 output, so the second workload uses an inconsistent prompt-only basis.
evidence: 2.62 MB/token × 1,300 tokens = 3,406 MB ≈ 3.41 GB. Canonical row: 2.62 × 9,500 = 24.9 GB max.
root_cause: Inconsistent KV basis: prompt-only in the second workload vs max context in the canonical table.
correction: Use 2.62 MB × 1,300 ≈ 3.41 GB for max KV, or label 1.05 GB as prompt-only and compare it to 24.1 GB prompt-only.
acceptance_test: Both workloads use the same KV basis; recomputation from 400+900 and 9,200+300 matches the printed values.

quoted_clause: this 30× ratio pushes the design toward high prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure
observed: KV capacity is driven by absolute context length and model architecture, not by the input/output ratio. A 9.2K/9.2K workload has ratio 1 but the same KV capacity as 9.2K/300 at the same total context.
evidence: KV bytes = 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes; the input/output ratio does not appear. The canonical 9.2K input drives KV; the 30× ratio drives prefill-vs-decode balance.
root_cause: Conflates ratio with absolute input length.
correction: Attribute KV pressure to the 9.2K context length; use the 30× ratio only for prefill/decode balance.
acceptance_test: The sentence separates ratio effects from absolute-context effects; a counterexample with ratio 1 and the same context is not contradicted.

quoted_clause: The shard-invariant reason decode is memory-limited is its low arithmetic intensity (~1.0 FLOP/byte)
observed: ~1.0 FLOP/byte is the batch-1 per-sequence intensity. At the canonical 10 rps, 300 output tokens, and 25 ms TPOT, concurrency is ~75, so weight reuse raises intensity to ~75 FLOP/byte (still below H100 ridge ~295, so memory-bound). The text presents ~1.0 as the system-level reason without stating batch.
evidence: Little's law: 10 rps × 300 tokens × 0.025 s = 75 concurrent sequences. Intensity ≈ batch × 1 FLOP/byte = 75 FLOP/byte. H100 ridge ≈ 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s ≈ 295 FLOP/byte.
root_cause: Uses batch-1 arithmetic intensity without qualifying batch/concurrency.
correction: State 'per-sequence at batch 1' or compute intensity at the canonical batch; explain batching raises intensity but remains below the ridge point.
acceptance_test: Arithmetic intensity is qualified by batch/concurrency and the memory-bound conclusion is re-derived at the canonical operating point.

quoted_clause: the 2 × params × tokens approximation may ignore activation reuse across batched requests
observed: Independent requests in a batch do not share activations; batching improves hardware utilization, not FLOP count. The 2NL approximation is not invalidated by cross-request activation reuse.
evidence: Each request has its own hidden states; no cross-request activation reuse occurs in standard batched inference. FLOPs remain 2N per token for dense models.
root_cause: Misconception about batching and activation reuse.
correction: Remove 'activation reuse across batched requests'; if discussing corrections, refer to kernel overhead, padding, or activation memory, not cross-request reuse.
acceptance_test: No claim of cross-request activation reuse; batching is described as utilization/efficiency, not FLOP reduction.

quoted_clause: moves the 2NL prefill term and the ~140 GB weight read in the same direction but not the KV-cache term, which depends on context length and layer count rather than parameter count
observed: A smaller dense model may have fewer layers or KV heads, so the KV-cache term can also shrink. Saying it does not move is misleading; it depends on layer count, KV-head count, head dimension, precision, and context length.
evidence: KV bytes = 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes. Layer count often scales with model size, so replacing the model can change KV.
root_cause: Overstates independence of KV from model size.
correction: Say the KV term depends on layer/KV-head geometry and context length and may or may not shrink with a smaller model; it is not tied to parameter count alone.
acceptance_test: The text acknowledges possible KV change when the model is replaced and lists the governing architecture variables.

quoted_clause: If prefill needs FLOPS and decode needs bandwidth, a single homogeneous GPU pool is suboptimal.
observed: The text later says P/D disaggregation depends on utilization, duplicated residency, KV-transfer cost, topology, workload shape, and burstiness. The unqualified 'is suboptimal' contradicts those caveats and overstates the case.
evidence: Same section: 'Whether it needs fewer GPUs ... depends on ... those effects must be measured before the GPU-count conclusion is drawn.'
root_cause: Universal claim where a conditional claim is supported.
correction: Change to 'can be suboptimal' or 'may leave performance on the table'; keep the later measurement caveats.
acceptance_test: The claim is qualified and consistent with the subsequent list of dependencies.

quoted_clause: Gate pass rate / false-promotion rate — how often a gated change later regresses in production; a rising value means the evaluation suite is losing fidelity.
observed: Gate pass rate and false-promotion rate are distinct. A rising gate pass rate can mean candidates are better or thresholds are looser; only a rising false-promotion rate directly indicates lost gate fidelity.
evidence: Pass rate = passed candidates / candidates; false-promotion rate = passed candidates that later regress / passed candidates. They have different denominators and causal meanings.
root_cause: Conflates two metrics under one definition.
correction: Define them separately: gate pass rate measures candidate throughput; false-promotion rate measures gate fidelity. Only the latter's rise implies lost fidelity.
acceptance_test: The two metrics have separate definitions and the causal claim is attached only to false-promotion rate.

page_hint: Ch 21 §3, 'Cost of a bad ungated release'
quoted_clause: the serving cost of the 216,000 requests exposed is ... (volume × unit rate — incurred whether or not the regression occurred)
observed: If the serving cost is incurred whether or not the regression occurred, it is baseline serving cost, not the incremental cost of the bad release. The heading 'Cost of a bad ungated release' then overstates what the $5,394/$3,032 figures represent.
evidence: The parenthetical explicitly says the cost is incurred regardless; the business cost of the regression is described separately as trust erosion and fire drill.
root_cause: Labels baseline cost as release cost.
correction: Rename the calculation 'baseline serving cost of the exposed requests' and separately state the incremental business cost is unquantified; or compute only incremental cost.
acceptance_test: The text distinguishes baseline serving cost from incremental bad-release cost; the heading matches the quantity computed.
